feedback: If a learner calls the Amazon a country or says it's only in Brazil, point back to the map: it's a rainforest that spans nine South American countries — trace its edges across more than one.
If a learner conflates the forest and the river, clarify: the forest is the habitat; the river runs through it.
Confirm correct country names against the map and invite them to find a second or third country they didn't expect.
activities.intendedInsight: The Amazon is Earth's greatest rainforest that crosses nine countries; it is a habitat, not a nation, and the river runs through the forest rather than being the same thing as it.
learnerActions: Locate the shaded Amazon basin on a map of South America.
Name at least two countries the Amazon spreads across (e.g. Brazil, Peru, Colombia).
State in your own words that the Amazon is a rainforest spanning nine South American countries — not a single country and not only Brazil.
activities.title: Find it on the map, then name the countries

feedback: If a learner justifies 'largest' only by length, redirect: here 'largest' means the most water carried (volume/discharge), not how long the river is.
Use the comparison bars to let them see the Amazon's bar dwarf the others and put the difference in their own words.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Largest river' in this topic means greatest water volume/discharge — the Amazon moves more water than the next several giant rivers combined — which is a distinct claim from how long a river is.
learnerActions: Consider the question 'Which river carries the most water on Earth?' and predict before the answer is shown.
Compare a thick bar representing the Amazon's water volume against bars for other major rivers (e.g. Nile, Mississippi) and describe what 'largest' means here.
State clearly that the Amazon is the largest river by water volume (discharge), and explain why this is different from being the longest.
activities.title: Largest by water, not by length

feedback: If a learner reads '10% of species' as '10 species', use the ten-Earths visual, where all ten pictures together stand for every known kind of life: shading one of the ten shows one tenth of ALL kinds of life. That is a huge number of distinct types, far more than 10. The plants alone are about 40,000 kinds.
If a learner says only 'many animals', push for variety: tens of thousands of different plant and animal types, not just high numbers of a few.
Treat the figures as estimates — tell learners many species are still undiscovered, so these numbers are approximate, not fixed exact counts.
activities.intendedInsight: Biodiversity is about the variety of distinct kinds of life; the Amazon holds about one tenth of all known species on Earth, an extraordinary concentration of different living things.
learnerActions: Look at a row of ten Earth pictures that together stand for all the known kinds of life on Earth, with each picture standing for one tenth. Shade one picture to show the roughly 10% of all those species that live in the Amazon.
Explain in your own words that this means roughly 1 in every 10 kinds of living thing on Earth lives here — not 10 species.
Read the record cards (about 40,000 plant species, 1,300 bird species, 3,000 types of fish) and name at least two specific biodiversity numbers.
Say why biodiversity means huge VARIETY of different kinds, not just 'lots of animals'.
activities.title: What '10% of all species' really means

feedback: If the learner keeps the Amazon as a country or only Brazil, reteach location on the map before the statistics.
If they say 'many animals' without variety, emphasise distinct kinds (~10% of all species).
If they give facts but no reason, prompt: what about the climate might let so many different kinds of life thrive here compared with, say, a British wood?
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who understands this topic can correct the country/length/scale errors and give a reason for the Amazon's biodiversity, not just recite facts.
learnerActions: Respond to the prompt: 'Someone says the Amazon is a country in Brazil. Is that right? Tell me what the Amazon actually is, and then why it's such a special place for wildlife.'
Give a corrected description: Earth's greatest rainforest across nine South American countries, with the largest river by water volume.
Explain WHY so much life lives there — linking the richness to the hot, wet climate rather than only restating numbers.
activities.title: Explain why the Amazon is special (diagnostic discussion)
